A kinsman is a male relative — a man who is connected to you through family. That's the heart of it. If a man shares a family bond with you, he is your kinsman.

The plural is kinsmen.
Who exactly counts as a kinsman?

Any male relative can be called your kinsman — there is no rule about how close or how distant the relationship must be.

Your kinsmen can include:

  • Close relatives: your father, brother, son, grandfather
  • More distant relatives: your uncle, cousin, nephew, or any other man further out on your family tree

The word doesn't draw a line. It simply names the fact that a family connection exists between you and that man.
The female equivalent and related words

Since "kinsman" specifically refers to a male relative, its female counterpart is kinswoman (plural: kinswomen).

When you want to refer to all your relatives together — both male and female — you use the word kin or kinsfolk (also spelled kinfolk). These are collective words that cover everyone in your family circle.

The abstract idea of being related — the state of sharing family bonds — is called kinship.

Mostly yes — "kinsman" almost always refers to someone related to you by blood (biological family). But in certain cultural, tribal, or historical settings, the word stretches slightly further:

  • In tribal or clan societies, men from the same tribe or clan often called each other kinsmen, even when the exact biological link was distant or unverifiable. The idea was that belonging to the same group made you family in a broad sense.
  • In some religious and community traditions, men from the same faith or ethnic group would sometimes use "kinsman" to signal solidarity and shared identity — the way you might call someone "brother" even when he isn't your literal brother.

This looser use is always rooted in the same idea: a bond that is like family, treated with the closeness and loyalty that family demands.
A special and important use: the kinsman-redeemer

In the Bible — especially in the Old Testament — the word "kinsman" carries a very specific and powerful meaning tied to duty and responsibility.

A kinsman-redeemer was the closest male relative of a person who had fallen into hardship. This kinsman had a legal and moral obligation to step in and rescue that family member. This duty could take several forms:

  • Buying back property that a relative had been forced to sell due to poverty, so the land stayed in the family
  • Marrying a widow (his deceased kinsman's wife) to carry on the family name and ensure she was cared for
  • Paying off a relative's debt to free him from bondage or servitude
  • Avenging a murdered relative — in ancient times, seeking justice for a kinsman's killing was considered a sacred duty

The most famous example in the Bible is the story of Ruth and Boaz. Ruth was a widow, and Boaz, being her late husband's close male relative, acted as her kinsman-redeemer by marrying her and protecting her future.

This concept shows that "kinsman" in its deepest historical use wasn't just a label — it came with obligations. To be someone's kinsman meant you were bound to protect them.

In everyday modern speech, you will almost never hear this word. People today simply say "relative," "family member," or name the specific relationship — "my uncle," "my cousin," and so on.

However, you will encounter "kinsman" quite regularly in:

  • The Bible and other religious scriptures — it appears frequently throughout both the Old and New Testaments
  • Classic literature — Shakespeare, older novels, and poetry use it often
  • Historical fiction — writers depicting ancient, medieval, or tribal settings reach for this word naturally
  • Formal speeches and oratory — especially in solemn or ceremonial contexts, a speaker might refer to "my kinsmen" to invoke a sense of shared heritage
  • Legal texts — older legal documents sometimes use it when discussing family rights and inheritance

So while it has largely stepped out of casual conversation, the word is very much alive wherever older or more formal language is used.

Here are a few examples showing how the word is used in context:

  • "He crossed the valley to seek help from a kinsman who lived in the northern village."
  • "The warrior swore an oath to avenge his fallen kinsman."
  • "Boaz was a kinsman of her husband's family, a man of great wealth."
  • "Even in a foreign land, he was welcomed warmly, for his host recognized him as a kinsman from the same tribe."
  • "She wrote to her last surviving kinsman, begging him to come to her aid."

A kinsman is simply a male relative. It can refer to anyone from your father to a distant cousin — any man tied to you by family. Beyond the literal family sense, it can extend to men of the same tribe, clan, or community in settings where those bonds are treated as family. In its most historically charged use (especially in the Bible), a kinsman was not just a relative but a protector — someone with a duty to rescue and redeem family members in need. Today the word lives mainly in literature, scripture, and formal or historical contexts, but its meaning has never changed: a man who is your family.
